marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q012.takeaway: Most axons from the lateral geniculate nucleus terminate in layer 4 of primary visual cortex, which lies around the calcarine fissure and has six neocortical layers. Layer 4 subdivides into 4A, 4B, 4Cα, and 4Cβ. LGN magnocellular layers 1–2 project to 4Cα, while parvocellular layers 3–6 project to 4Cβ.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q013.takeaway: A protanope has red-color deficiency (protanopia) and is a dichromat, with only two functioning cone systems. The analogous green and blue deficiencies are deuteranopia and tritanopia. Anomalous trichromacy describes altered function in one cone system while retaining three classes. The source also associates color blindness with X-linked inheritance and cortical achromatopsia with lesions of visual area V8.

Protanopia is the red-deficiency form of dichromatic color vision.

Source explanation detail: Protanopes are dichromats with difficulty in identifying red color.

+ Dichromatic Vision (Individuals with only two cone systems)
+ Blindness to red color Protanopia (Protanope).
+ Blindness to green color Deuteranopia (Deuteranope).
+ Blindness to blue color Tritanopia (Tritanope).
* Monochromatic Vision Have only one cone system.
+ Color blindness is X-linked recessive.

rationales.b: Green deficiency is deuteranopia (or deuteranomaly in anomalous trichromacy), not protanopia.
rationales.c: Blue deficiency is tritanopia (or tritanomaly), not protanopia.
rationales.d: Black is not the color deficiency defined by protanopia; the source pairs protanopia with red.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q014.takeaway: The medial geniculate nucleus is the thalamic auditory relay from brainstem pathways to primary auditory cortex. The lateral geniculate nucleus is the corresponding major thalamic relay for visual information. The item asks for the auditory, not visual or somatosensory, thalamic relay.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q014.displayText:
Auditory information reaches cortex through the medial geniculate nucleus.

Source explanation detail: ‘The medial geniculate nucleus is the thalamic nucleus that conveys auditory information from the
brainstem to the primary auditory cortex.
Lateral geniculate nucleus is the thalamic nucleus that conveys visual information.

rationales.a: The dorsomedial nucleus is not the source's auditory relay; that pathway is assigned to the medial geniculate nucleus.
rationales.b: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays visual information, rather than auditory information.
rationales.d: The ventral posterolateral nucleus is a somatosensory relay for the body, not the auditory thalamic relay.

Its lateral division compares interaural intensity differences; its medial division detects interaural timing differences. Cochlear-nucleus projections reach both ipsilateral and contralateral superior olives, enabling these binaural comparisons.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q016.takeaway: Loudness increases as basilar-membrane vibration amplitude rises. Hair cells then excite auditory-nerve endings at higher rates, and the larger vibration recruits hair cells at the edges of the resonating region. At high intensity, outer hair cells are recruited substantially. Thus the defining event among these choices is increased basilar-membrane amplitude.

Greater basilar-membrane vibration amplitude signals a louder sound.

rationales.a: Loudness recruits more, not fewer, hair cells as basilar-membrane vibration grows.
rationales.b: Outer hair-cell recruitment increases at high intensity; a decrease would run opposite to the source's description.
rationales.c: Hair cells excite auditory-nerve endings more rapidly as sound intensity and membrane amplitude rise.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q017.takeaway: Umami is evoked especially by glutamate, including monosodium glutamate. The source lists five basic tastes (sweet, salt, sour, bitter, umami) and distinguishes ligand-gated channels for salt and sour from G-protein-coupled receptors for sweet, bitter, and umami. It identifies T1R2/T1R3 for sweet, a taste-receptor family for bitter, and metabotropic glutamate receptor mGluR4 for umami. The keyed distinction is glutamate; source details on specific receptor families are retained as its account.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q017.displayText: Glutamate is the stimulus associated with umami taste.

rationales.a: Glucose is associated with sweet taste, rather than the glutamate cue for umami.
rationales.b: Quinine is a classic bitter stimulus; bitter is distinct from glutamate-associated umami.
rationales.d: Sodium chloride provides a salt stimulus; the keyed umami stimulus is glutamate.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q018.takeaway: Mitral and tufted cells in the olfactory bulb receive olfactory-nerve input in glomeruli and form second-order neurons that project to olfactory cortex. The bulb also contains inhibitory periglomerular interneurons and granule cells; granule cells make reciprocal synapses with mitral and tufted cells. These cell types belong to olfactory circuitry rather than the cardiac, visual, or geniculate structures offered as distractors.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q019.takeaway: Olfaction has a comparatively small range over which intensity is discriminated. Smell is especially effective for detecting whether an odor is present; concentrations only about 10–50 times threshold may produce maximal perceived intensity, unlike systems that encode a broad range of stimulus magnitudes.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q019.displayText:
Olfaction is better at detecting odor presence than grading a wide intensity range.

Source explanation detail: ‘The olfactory system has the smallest range of intensity discrimination.
Smell is concerned more with detecting the presence or absence of odors , than with the
quantitative detection of their intensities. Concentrations that are only 10 to 50 times above
threshold values will evoke maximum intensity of smell, which is in contrast to most other

sensory system of the body.

rationales.a: Audition can discriminate sound intensity over a wider range than olfaction in this comparison.
rationales.b: Vision encodes graded changes in illumination over a larger intensity range than the olfactory system described here.
rationales.d: Somatosensation can encode stimulus magnitude over a broader range; odor intensity saturates relatively close to threshold.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q020.takeaway: Each human eye has approximately 6 million cones and 120 million rods. Rods and cones each have outer and inner segments, a nuclear region, and a synaptic zone; photosensitive pigments occupy discs or saccules in the outer segment. Dark adaptation after moving from bright to dim conditions approaches its maximum over about 20 minutes, whereas light adaptation after moving from dim to bright takes about 5 minutes.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q020.displayText: There are about 6 million cones in each eye; rods are far more numerous.

rationales.b: Five to twelve million exceeds the source estimate; it gives approximately 6 million cones per eye.
rationales.c: Ten to fifteen million is substantially above the stated cone count of about 6 million.
rationales.d: Twenty million is far above the source estimate for cones; approximately 120 million is the rod count.

marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q021.takeaway: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil refers to a light-reflex abnormality in which illuminating the blind half of the retina elicits no pupillary response, while stimulating the intact retinal half does. It is associated with optic-tract lesions; the source also notes optic-thalamic disease such as tuberculosis, syphilis, or tumors. Homonymous hemianopia follows lesions posterior to the optic chiasm, producing loss of the same visual-field half in both eyes.
marrow__PHYS_CH13_Q021.displayText: Wernicke's hemianopic pupil is associated with an optic-tract lesion.

rationales.a: An optic-nerve lesion interrupts afferent input from the affected eye rather than causing the hemianopic half-retina pattern described.
rationales.c: An optic-radiation lesion can cause homonymous field loss but is posterior to the tract; the source keys the hemianopic pupil to the optic tract.
rationales.d: An optic-chiasm lesion classically affects crossing nasal fibers and does not match the keyed optic-tract site.
